strengths: The central empirical hypothesis (Store-Contribute Dissociation) is intuitive and well-motivated conceptually, drawing a useful distinction between representation storage (teacher similarity) and functional/causal contribution (ablation-induced velocity change) that is under-explored in the REPA literature for audio.

The forward-only gate ablation (FoG-A) provides a simple, interpretable causal attribution signal that is directly actionable for layer selection, and the paper connects it to a residual-Jacobian sensitivity argument for intuition.

Table 3's comparison of layer-selection strategies (random, highest-LASP, gradient-norm, FoG-A) is a good controlled ablation that isolates the value of the causal-attribution criterion versus simpler alternatives and versus storage-based selection.

The paper reports results across two token-conditioning topologies (Config A/B) and claims generalization to three additional Flow Matching architectures (Voicebox, CosyVoice, F5-TTS), which if fully substantiated would strengthen the case for broad applicability.

The probe-then-intervene protocol (freezing layer selection after a diagnostic warm-up before comparing baseline vs. AG-REPA) is a reasonable design choice to avoid circular optimization/leakage concerns.
weaknesses: Training budgets described in Appendix A.5 are extremely short (1 warm-up epoch + 2 additional epochs) for training large unified LLM+DiT audio systems on LibriSpeech+AudioSet; it is unclear whether conclusions drawn from such limited training generalize to fully converged models, and no justification is given for why 2-3 epochs is sufficient to draw strong causal claims.

Most quantitative tables (Table 1, Table 3, and WER/FAD columns of Table 2 and Table 4) report single-run point estimates without variance/confidence intervals, despite the paper claiming results are 'averaged over three distinct seeds'; this omission makes it impossible to assess whether the reported gains (e.g., 18%/16% FAD reduction) are statistically meaningful versus training noise.

The generalization experiments in Table 4 applying AG-REPA to Voicebox, CosyVoice, and F5-TTS are described with minimal methodological detail (no description of how FoG-A was computed for these architectures, training length, hyperparameters, or compute budget), and the suspiciously uniform, clean improvements across three unrelated architectures raise reproducibility concerns.

The theoretical section (Sec. 3) largely restates well-known facts about residual networks and Jacobian sensitivity (e.g., Veit et al.'s ensemble-of-shallow-networks view) without deriving audio- or flow-matching-specific predictions; the connection between the generic 'Butterfly Effect' argument and the specific empirical finding that Layer 1 dominates is asserted rather than rigorously established.

No direct quantitative comparison to competing REPA refinements discussed in Related Work (HASTE, iREPA, TARO, HunyuanVideo-Foley) is provided in the main results, despite these being positioned as the closest related methods; the paper only compares against naive fixed-layer REPA baselines.

The paper introduces a fairly heavy three-part diagnostic toolkit (BiT-C, LASP, FoG-A) plus a two-stage LLM+DiT system, which increases complexity and the surface area for undisclosed implementation choices, while the core methodological contribution (top-K attribution-weighted layer selection for REPA) is relatively incremental over standard REPA.

Figure 1's heatmap, central to establishing the paper's main empirical claim, is presented before the methodology (BiT-C/LASP/FoG-A) is formally introduced in Section 4, and the exact experimental configuration (model size, dataset subset, number of samples) used to produce it is not clearly specified, limiting reproducibility of the key motivating result.

strengths: The central idea—dissociating representational storage (LASP) from functional/causal contribution (FoG-A) via a Jacobian/residual argument—is a clean, interpretable framing that connects prior interpretability literature (Klabunde et al., Braun et al., Hase et al.) to a concrete, actionable training method for REPA in audio flow matching.

The forward-only gate ablation (FoG-A) is simple, cheap (<0.5% wall-clock overhead as claimed), and gives a practical causal-attribution signal rather than relying purely on gradient norms or teacher similarity.

Extensive ablations are provided: sensitivity to K and weighting scheme, static vs. timestep-adaptive alignment, projection-head design (MLP vs conv), internal self-alignment vs external teachers, and stability of the selected layer set across training checkpoints.

The comparison against multiple informative baselines (fixed single-layer REPA, multi-layer heuristic, Deep REPA, Shallow REPA, random/gradient-norm layer selection) helps isolate the source of the reported gains and supports the core claim that causal attribution outperforms storage-based selection within their own setup.
MOS evaluation includes a defined rater protocol and paired significance testing, which is good practice relative to many generative-audio papers that report only point estimates.
weaknesses: The 'mechanistic' theory in Section 3 is largely qualitative and is explicitly acknowledged as not being a proof (Section 3.2); it also predicts, essentially by construction of the residual/Jacobian telescoping argument, that early layers will have larger downstream influence in any residual network, regardless of audio-specific properties. This makes it unclear whether the reported dominance of Layer 1 reflects an audio-specific insight or a generic property of residual/DiT architectures that would be observed in any modality, weakening the novelty of the SCD claim as an audio-specific contribution.

The cross-architecture generalization experiments (Voicebox, CosyVoice, F5-TTS in Table 4/5) lack sufficient methodological detail: it is unclear whether these are retrained from scratch, fine-tuned, over what data/budget, and how FoG-A/AG-REPA was integrated into each external codebase. Given these are large, previously published systems, the absence of implementation specifics raises reproducibility concerns and makes the generalization claims difficult to verify.

No code, model checkpoints, or audio samples are provided, and key architectural details (model size, number of parameters, exact number of layers used across configs, compute budget) are not clearly specified in the main text, limiting reproducibility.

Statistical rigor is uneven: WER/FAD are averaged over only 3 seeds with no significance testing (acknowledged by authors as insufficient), while only MOS receives a formal significance test; this makes the primary objective metrics (FAD reductions of 18%/16% highlighted in the abstract) less rigorously supported than the framing suggests.

The paper does not compare against existing audio-domain REPA adaptations mentioned in related work (TARO, HunyuanVideo-Foley) as empirical baselines, despite discussing them at length; all baselines are internal ablations on the authors' own architecture (aside from the generalization experiments), which somewhat limits the strength of the comparison to prior art.

The improvements, while consistent, are incremental in absolute terms (e.g., FAD 1.36→1.29 for Shallow REPA vs AG-REPA), and the paper does not discuss potential trade-offs or failure cases where attribution-guided selection might underperform simpler heuristics, nor does it discuss variance/robustness of the FoG-A ranking under different initialization seeds beyond checkpoint stability.
